candidates.text: "For seeing our race grown numerous enough, King Pharaoh devised much guile against us, torturing some mortals at the brick-making and the heavy buildings, and walling cities, for the sake of his own ill-fated ends. Then he proclaimed to us, the race of the Hebrews, to cast the males into the deep-flowing river. Here my mother who bore me hid me three months, as she said; but, not escaping notice, she put me secretly away, having wrapped a covering about me, by the river's edge, in the deep, shaggy marsh. And Mariam my sister kept watch nearby; and then the king's daughter came down with her maids, to brighten her young skin with bathing. And seeing me at once, and pitying me, she took me up, and knew that I was a Hebrew; and Mariam my sister, running up, says this to the princess: 'Do you wish that I find for you quickly a nurse for this child from among the Hebrews?' And she urged on the girl. And going, she told my mother, and quickly she was present, my mother herself, and took me in her arms. And the king's daughter said: 'Nurse this one, woman, and I will give you your wage.' And she named the name Moses, for the reason that she took me up from the watery river-bank. And when the time of infancy had passed for me, my mother brought me to the princess's halls, having told me everything in story and recounted to me my father's race and the gifts of God. And so, as long as we had the time of childhood, she promised everything by royal rearings and trainings, as though from her own womb. But when the full circle of days was at hand, I went out of the royal house."

out of such strifes and groans you were born.

Earth nurtures nothing feebler than a man.
Best of all for men on earth is never to be born,

We ought, when a man is born, to gather together

Blessed is he who has seen those things and so goes beneath the earth;

And then I bear children amid bitter pains;

What good is this? Is it not enough
to vex one single soul, and then to have toils upon it?
To me it seems, now as long ago,
O you who were born to be wretched and to fare ill,

neither by burning, nor by letting down terrible saws
from the top of my head to my feet's ends,
could you learn, nor if you should put all bonds upon me,
For it was not Zeus who proclaimed these things to me;
There is a saying
that Virtue dwells upon rocks hard to climb,

and that the swift, holy chorus of nymphs attends her;
nor is she to be seen by the eyes of all mortals,
save by the one in whom heart-biting sweat comes from within,
and who reaches the summit by manliness.
The cares of the young, whirled about with toils,
find glory; and in time their works
shine, kindled above the heavens.

13.101. And the lyric poet: "And it is possible for God, out of black night, to raise an unstained light, and with dark cloudy gloom to cover the pure brightness of the day" (for the one who alone, while day is present, can make night, this, he says, is God); and in the work entitled Phaenomena, Aratus, having said, "Let us begin from Zeus," whom, O men, we never leave unspoken, adds: "and full of Zeus are all the streets, and all the gatherings of men, full too the sea and the harbours; everywhere we all have need of Zeus. For we are also his offspring" — that is, his creation; "and gentle to men he gives favourable signs, and stirs the peoples to work; and these signs he fixed in the heaven, distinguishing the stars; and he looked out, against the year, for stars that should most surely signify to men the things of the seasons, that all might grow firm; and him men ever propitiate first and last: hail, Father, great wonder, great help to men." And before him Homer too, fashioning the world after Moses upon the shield wrought by Hephaestus, says: "On it he made the earth, and on it the heaven, and on it the sea, and on it all the constellations with which heaven is crowned." For the Zeus sung of in the poems and in the prose writings carries the conception up to God.

13.107. But the seventh day, too, is held sacred not only by the Hebrews but by the Greeks, according to which the whole world of all things that are quickened and grow goes round. Hesiod, then, speaks of it thus: "First the new moon and the fourth, and the seventh, a holy day." And again: "On the seventh again the bright light of the sun." And Homer: "On the seventh thereupon came the holy day." And: "The seventh was holy." And again: "It was the seventh day, and on it all was accomplished." And again: "On the seventh dawn we left the stream from Acheron." Indeed Callimachus the poet too writes: "On the seventh dawn, and on it all things were fashioned." And again: "Among good things is the seventh, and the seventh is the birthday." And: "The seventh is among the first, and the seventh is perfect." And: "Seven were all the things made in the starry heaven, appearing in their circles as the years come round."

13.109. Well, then, does Xenophanes of Colophon, teaching that God is one and incorporeal, add: "One God, greatest among gods and men, in no way like to mortals, neither in body nor in mind." And again: "But mortals think that the gods are born, and have their own raiment and voice and shape." And again: "But if oxen or lions had hands, so as to draw with their hands and accomplish such works as men, then horses would draw the forms of gods like horses, and oxen like oxen, and would make their bodies such as each itself had."
13.110. Let us hear again Bacchylides the lyric poet speaking of the divine: "They are untamed of unseemly diseases, and unharmed, in no way like to men." And Cleanthes the Stoic, having written these things about God in a certain poem: "You ask me what the Good is like? Hear, then: ordered, just, holy, pious, master of itself, useful, beautiful, fitting, austere, downright, ever profitable, fearless, painless, advantageous, free of grief, beneficial, well-pleasing, secure, friendly, honoured, consistent, . . . of good repute, free of conceit, careful, gentle, strong, lasting, blameless, ever-abiding."

13.113. Sophocles, as Hecataeus, who composed the histories, says in his work On Abraham and the Egyptians, cries out plainly upon the stage: "One in very truth, one is God, who made the heaven and the broad earth, and the grey-green swell of the sea, and the strength of the winds. But we mortals, many, wandering in heart, set up for ourselves a comfort in our pains — images of the gods made of stones, or of bronze, or of figures wrought of gold or ivory; and decking these with sacrifices and vain festivals, we think thus we are pious."
13.118. And the comic poet Epicharmus speaks plainly of the Word in his Republic, somewhat thus: "Life has very great need for man of reckoning and number; we live by number and reckoning, for these save mortals." Then he downright adds: "Reason governs men, and saves them in their measure." Then: "If there is reckoning in man, there is also a divine reason. The one in man is born for the conduct of life; but the divine reason attends upon all the arts, itself teaching men what they must do for their advantage. For man did not find out an art, but God brings it; and the reason in man is sprung from the divine reason."

13.119. Indeed, when the Spirit cries out through Isaiah, "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord; I am full of whole-burnt-offerings of rams, and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls I do not want"; and a little after adds, "Wash yourselves, become clean, take away the wickednesses from your souls," and the things that follow — Menander the comic poet writes in these very words: "If anyone, O Pamphilus, bringing a sacrifice — a multitude of bulls or of kids, or, by Zeus, of other such things, or fashionings, having made golden cloaks or purple ones, or figures of ivory or emerald — thinks to make God well-disposed, he is deceived and has a feather-light mind. For a man must be of use, not corrupting maidens nor committing adultery, not stealing and slaughtering for the sake of money. Nor covet even the thread of a needle, friend; for God sees you, being present near at hand." "I am a God who draws near, and not a God afar off; or shall a man do anything in secret, and I shall not see him?" he says through Jeremiah.

13.120. And again Menander, paraphrasing that Scripture, "Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope upon the Lord," writes somewhat thus: "Never covet, dearest, even a needle that belongs to another; for God delights in righteous deeds, and not in unjust ones, and suffers the man who toils to lift up his own life, ploughing the earth night and day. To God sacrifice continually, being righteous, not splendid in your cloaks so much as in your heart. If you hear thunder, do not flee, conscious of no evil within yourself, O master; for God sees you, being present near at hand." "While you are still speaking," says the Scripture, "I will say, Behold, I am here."
13.121. Again Diphilus the comic poet discourses thus concerning the judgement: "Do you think, Niceratus, that the dead, who have partaken of all luxury in life, have escaped the divine as though unobserved? There is an eye of Justice that sees all things. For we believe there are two paths in Hades — one of the just, the other of the impious. And if the earth shall cover both for all time, then go off and plunder, steal, despoil, throw all into confusion; but be deceived in nothing — there is a judgement even in Hades, which God will hold, the master of all, whose name is fearful, and which I would not even name. He gives to those who sin a long span of life. And if any mortal thinks that, doing some evil by day, he has escaped the gods, he is convicted of thinking wickedly, and of being so, whenever Justice chances to have leisure. Look, all you who think there is no God: there is, there is. And if any man, being evil by nature, does well, let him gain the time; for in time, afterward, he will pay the penalty." And tragedy sings in tune with these things by these words: "For there shall be, there shall be, that time of the age, when the golden-faced aether shall let loose its treasury full of fire, and the nursed flame, raging, shall burn up all things upon earth and on high."

13.123. The same Orpheus says these things too: "Looking to the divine Word, attend upon it, guiding straight the intelligent vessel of your heart; and walk well in the path, and gaze upon the immortal Ruler of the world alone." And again concerning God, calling him invisible, he says he was made known to one only, a Chaldean by race — whether he means Abraham, or his Son — by these words: "Except one only, a scion sprung from the stock of the Chaldeans from above; for he knew the path of the star, and the movement of the sphere round the earth, how it revolves in a circle, evenly upon its own axle, and he guides the winds about the air and about the stream."
13.124. Then, paraphrasing, as it were, "The heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet," he goes on: "But he himself, again, is fixed upon the great heaven on a golden throne, and the earth has gone beneath his feet; and his right hand he has stretched out to the bounds of Ocean; and the base of the mountains trembles within at his wrath, nor can it bear his mighty force. And he is everywhere heavenly, and on earth he accomplishes all things, himself holding beginning and middle and end. In no other way is it lawful for you to speak; and my limbs tremble in my mind. From on high he sways," and the rest. For by these things he has shown forth all those prophetic words: "If you open the heaven, trembling shall seize the mountains from before you, and they shall melt, as wax melts before the face of fire."

13.125. And the words through Isaiah: "Who measured the heaven with a span, and the whole earth with a handful?" Again, when he says: "Lord of aether and Hades, of sea and earth, who with your thunders shakes the strong dwelling of Olympus; before whom the spirits shudder, and the throng of gods is afraid; whom the Fates obey, inexorable though they are; imperishable one, mother-and-father, by whose passion all things are stirred; you who move the winds, and cover all with clouds, cleaving the broad aether with your lightnings; yours is the order among the stars, running upon unchangeable behests; and beside your fiery throne stand the much-toiling angels, whose care it is that all things be accomplished for mortals; yours is the spring that shines new with purple flowers; yours the winter that comes on with chill clouds; your fruits the reveller Bromius once distributed."

13.128. Well, then, does Philemon the comic poet also cut down idolatry, by these words: "There is for us no Fortune that is a god, there is none; but the chance thing that comes to pass for each as it happens is called fortune." And Sophocles the tragedian: "Not even for the gods," he says, "are all things self-willed, save for Zeus; for he holds the end and the beginning." And Orpheus: "One power, one spirit there came to be, a great one, kindling heaven; and one are all things made, in which all these things wheel round — fire and water and earth."
13.132. Besides these, Apollo, the most oracular, witnessing to the glory of God, is constrained to speak concerning Athena, at the time when the Medes were marching against Hellas, how she besought and supplicated Zeus on behalf of Attica. The oracle runs thus: "Pallas cannot propitiate Olympian Zeus, though she entreat with many words and shrewd counsel; but many temples of the immortals he will give over to the devouring fire — temples that even now, perhaps, stand streaming with sweat, quaking with terror," and the rest.

13.137. And Pindar downright brings in Zeus the Saviour too, dwelling with Themis, the king, the saviour, the just, interpreting somewhat thus: "First the well-counselling heavenly Themis, with golden horses, beside the streams of Ocean, the Fates led up to the august stairway of Olympus, along the shining way, to be the ancient consort of Zeus the Saviour; and she bore the gold-crowned, bright-fruited, true Hours." He, then, who is not persuaded by the truth, but puffed up with human teaching, is ill-fated and wretched, and, according to Euripides, "he who, beholding these things, perceives not God, and has cast far off the crooked deceits of those who babble of things on high, whose ruinous tongue casts at random concerning the unseen, having no share of judgement."
16.144. "With seven-toned lyre we shall sing new hymns," a poet of no mean note writes, teaching too that the old lyre was seven-noted. And seven too are the organs of the senses set about our face — two of the eyes, two of the channels of hearing, two of the nostrils, and the seventh that of the mouth. And that the changes of the ages come about by hebdomads, the elegies of Solon make plain, somewhat thus: "A boy, while still a child, ungrown, having grown the hedge of his teeth, casts the first within seven years; and when God has completed the second seven years, he shows forth the tokens of coming youth; in the third, while his limbs are growing, his chin is downed, his skin changing its bloom; and in the fourth, every man is greatest in strength, which men hold for the tokens of manhood; in the fifth, it is time for a man to be mindful of marriage, and to seek a generation of children thereafter; in the sixth, the mind of a man is fitted in all things, and he no longer wishes to do vain deeds; and in the seventh, he is greatest in mind and tongue, and in the eighth — fourteen years in both; in the ninth, he is still able, but his body and strength are more moderate toward great virtue; and in the tenth, when God has completed seven years, he would not be untimely in having his portion of death."

The Assembly of Stars
As the sun departed, it struck the black-robed evening,
Pelting it with tulips from the platter of the horizon.
The twilight adorned her with jewels of pure gold,
While Nature removed all her ornaments of silver.
In the palanquin of silence, the dark maiden of the night arrived,
And the lovely pearls of the Bride of the Night began to shine.
Those who dwell far from the world’s great tumult,
Whom humanity, in its own tongue, calls 'the stars.'
The celestial assembly was absorbed in illuminating the heavens,
When from the Highest Heaven came the voice of an angel:
“O guardians of the night, O stars of the sky,
Your entire nation, dwelling in the firmament, is luminous!
“Strike up such a melody that the sleepers may awaken;
The light of your brows is a guide for caravans.

This ground that witnessed the steps of the Prophet's successors?
This is that garden whose every bud was a garden in itself;
This is the final tomb of those before whom Rome would tremble.
The land of Cordoba, too, is the light of a Muslim's eye,
A Lamp of Sinai that shone in the darkness of the West.
Its flame went out, and scattered the Shining Nation's assembly,
Yet in its dying breath, it lit the lamp of the civilization of today.
This sacred land is the tomb of that civilization,
From which the vine of Europe's garden drew its very lifeblood.
The realm of Constantinople, once the abode of Caesar,
Now an eternal symbol of the Ummah's power and grandeur.
Like the dust of the Holy Sanctuary, this land is also pure;
It is the threshold of a throne that serves the Lord of Creation's Purpose.

It sings in nightingales, in buds unseen.
Come! I will show its radiant face to you,
In river-mirrors and the glass of dew.
In deserts, plains, and on the mountain's height,
Within Man's heart, and in your face's light.
A word that from the heart begins its flight,
Though featherless, it soars to awesome height.
Of holy stock, it seeks the lofty spheres,
From dust it rises, and through heavens steers.
My Passion was a rebel, sharp and sly,
My fearless wail went ripping through the sky.
The Ancient of the Skies then spoke: “Who calls?”
The planets whispered, “From the highest walls
Of Heaven’s Throne, a voice descends to hear.”
The Moon replied, “No, from the earthly sphere.”
But only Heaven’s Guardian understood;

The tent of heaven stands on this decree;
The pulse of being, throbbing, hot, and fast,

It lives in deserts, on the mountain’s face,

"Ah, Yathrib!" in his heart, on his lips, the One God's creed.
Fear speaks: "To Yathrib's gates, do not now dare to tread."
But Passion cries: "You are a Muslim! Go without dread!"
Shall I turn back to God's own House, my visit left undone?
And on the Day of Reckoning, the lovers' gazes shun?
The wanderer of Hejaz has no fear of death's abyss;
The secret of the Hijra of Yathrib's tomb is this.
Though safety's with the Syrian train, a guarded, steady ride,
The bliss of Passion lives where mortal risks abide.
Ah! This calculating Reason, how cunningly it's made,
And yet the soul of man, how bold and unafraid!
The Philosophy of Sorrow
Though life's own wine is filled with joyful glee,
Its clouds hold tears for every soul to see.
Upon the waves of Sorrow, life's frail bubble rides,

If the beloved's parting meant Annihilation's art,
Then passion's fire would also flee the loving, grieving heart.
Love does not perish when the one beloved has passed away,
It lives within the soul as Sorrow, and is there to stay.
From Love's own Permanence, the loved one's being is secured,
Their life knows not oblivion, their presence is assured.
A river from the mountain's brow comes singing on its way,
And teaches birds of heaven songs to brighten up the day.
Its mirror shines as brightly as a heavenly maiden's face,
Then shatters on the valley rocks throughout that rugged space.
What was a stream becomes a thousand pearls of lovely sheen,
As from that fall, a million stars of water can be seen.
The flowing stream of mercury is scattered and undone,
A world of restless, anxious drops appears beneath the sun.

A star looks on, of faint and greenish hue.
It sees the world, a game of dust and strife,

GETA:
I, too, did all I could.
ANTIPHO:

DORIO:
Now, do prate on.
PHAEDRIA:
For you to be of a disposition so harsh and inexorable, that neither by pity nor by entreaties can you be softened!
DORIO:
For you to be of a disposition so unreasonable and so unconscionable, Phaedria, that you can be talking me over with fine words, and be for amusing yourself with what’s my property for nothing!
ANTIPHO:
(apart, to GETA.)
I am sorry for him.
PHAEDRIA:
(aside.)
Alas! I feel it to be too true.
GETA:
(apart, to ANTIPHO.)
How well each keeps up to his character!
PHAEDRIA:

ANTIPHO:
Geta, shall we suffer him to continue thus wretched, when he so lately assisted me in the kind way you were mentioning? On the contrary, why not, as there’s need of it try to do him a kindness in return?
GETA:
For my part, I’m sure it is but fair.
ANTIPHO:
Come then, you are the only man able to serve him.
GETA:
What can I do?
ANTIPHO:
Procure the money.
GETA:
I wish I could; but where it is to come from—tell me that.
ANTIPHO:
My father has come home.
GETA:
I know; but what of that?

CHREMES:
Why, faith, a malady detained me.
DEMIPHO:
From what cause? Or what was it?
CHREMES:
Do you ask me?
Old age itself is a malady. However, I heard that they had arrived safe, from the caps tain who brought them.
DEMIPHO:
Have you heard, Chremes, what has happened to my son in my absence?
CHREMES:
’Tis that, in fact, that has embarrassed me in my plans. For if I offer my daughter in marriage to any person that’s a stranger, it must all be told how and by whom I had her. You I knew to be fully as faithful to me as I am to myself; if a stranger shall think fit to be connected with me by marriage, he will hold his tongue, just as long as good terms exist between us: but if he takes a dislike to me, he’ll be knowing more than it’s proper he should know.
I am afraid, too, lest my wife should, by some means, come to know of it; if that is the case, it only remains for me to shake myself and leave the house; for I’m the only one I can rely on at home.

At first the fellow raved.
DEMIPHO:
Say, what did he ask?
GETA:
What? A great deal too much.
CHREMES:
How much? Tell me.
GETA:
Suppose he were to give a great talent.
DEMIPHO:
Aye, faith, perdition to him rather; has he no shame?
GETA:
Just what I said to him: Pray, said I, suppose he was portioning an only daughter of his own. It has been of little benefit that he hasn’t one of his own, when another has been found to be demanding a fortune. To be brief, and to pass over his impertinences, this at last was his final answer:
I, said he, from the very first, have been desirous to marry the daughter of my friend, as was fit I should; for I was aware of the ill results of this, a poor wife being married into a rich family, and becoming a slave. But, as I am now conversing with you unreservedly,

ANTIPHO:
I only wish it may be the case.
GETA:
It shall be the case; trust me for that. Your father’s coming out; go tell Phaedria that the money is found.
(Enter DEMIPHO and CHREMES, from the house of the latter, the former with a purse of money.)
DEMIPHO:
Do be quiet, I tell you; I’ll take care he shall not be playing any tricks upon us. I’ll not rashly part with this without having my witnesses;
I’ll have it stated to whom I pay it, and for what purpose I pay it.
GETA:
(apart.)
How cautious he is, when there’s no need for it!
CHREMES:
Why yes, you had need do so, and with all haste, while the fit is upon him; for if this other woman shall prove more pressing, perhaps he may throw us over.
GETA:
You’ve hit upon the very thing.
DEMIPHO:

Look round at me.
SOPHRONA:
(seeing him.)
Ye Gods, I do beseech you, isn’t this Stilpho?
CHREMES:
No.
SOPHRONA:
Do you deny it?
CHREMES:
(in a low voice.)
Step a little this way from that door, Sophrona, if you please (pointing). Don’t you, henceforth, be calling me by that name.
SOPHRONA:
Why? Pray, are you not the person you always used to say you were?
CHREMES:
Hush! (pointing to his own house.)
SOPHRONA:

(Goes into the house of DEMIPHO.)
(Enter DEMIPHO and NAUSISTRATA, from the house of CHREMES.)
DEMIPHO:
Come now, Nausistrata, after your usual way, manage to keep her in good-humor with us, and make her do of her own accord what must be done.
NAUSISTRATA:
I will.
DEMIPHO:
You are now seconding me with your endeavors, just as you assisted me with your money before.
NAUSISTRATA:
I wish to do so; and yet, i’ faith, through the fault of my husband, I am less able than I ought to be.
DEMIPHO:
Why so?
NAUSISTRATA:
Because, i’ faith, he takes such indifferent care of the property that was so industriously acquired by my father; for from those farms he used regularly to receive two talents of silver yearly; there’s an instance, how superior one man is to another.
DEMIPHO:
Two talents, pray?

Do you persist?
NAUSISTRATA:
I wonder what all this can be.
DEMIPHO:
For my part, upon my faith, I don’t know.
CHREMES:
(whispering to him.)
Would you like to know? Then, so may Jupiter preserve me, not a person is there more nearly related to her than are you and I.
DEMIPHO:
(starting.)
Ye Gods, by our trust in you! let’s away to her; I wish for all of us, one way or other, to be sure about this (going).
CHREMES:
(stopping him.)
Ah!
DEMIPHO:
What’s the matter?

(apart to PHORMIO.)
Do you understand what he’s talking about?
PHORMIO:
(apart to ANTIPHO.)
Do you?
ANTIPHO:
(apart to PHORMIO.)
Not at all.
PHORMIO:
(apart to ANTIPHO.)
And I just as much.
GETA:
(to himself.)
I’ll be off hence to the Procurer’s; they are there just now. (Runs along.)
ANTIPHO:
(calling out.)

ANTIPHO:
O my dear Phormio, farewell!
PHORMIO:
Farewell, Antipho. (ANTIPHO and GETA go into DEMIPHO’S house.) So may the Gods bless me, this has turned out luckily. I’m glad of it, that such good fortune has thus suddenly befallen them.
I have now an excellent opportunity for diddling the old men, and ridding Phaedria of all anxiety about the money, so that he mayn’t be under the necessity of applying to any of his companions. For this same money, as it has been given him, shall be given for good, whether they like it or not: how to force them to this, I’ve found out the very way.
I must now assume a new air and countenance. But I’ll betake myself off to this next alley; from that spot I’ll present myself to them, when they come out of doors. I sha’n’t go to the fair, where I pretended I was going.

DEMIPHO:
Come before a magistrate. (Going to seize hold of him.)
PHORMIO:
Why, really, if you persist in being troublesome—
DEMIPHO:
What will you do?
PHORMIO:
What, I? You fancy, perhaps, just now, that I am the protector of the portionless; for the well portioned,
I’m in the habit of being so as well.
CHREMES:
What’s that to us?
PHORMIO:
(with a careless air.)
Nothing at all. I know a certain lady here (pointing at CHREMES’S house) whose husband had—
CHREMES:
(starting.)

CHREMES:
(aside.)
I am brought to such a pass, that I really don’t know what to do in it.
DEMIPHO:
I know; let’s go into court.
PHORMIO:
Into court? Here in preference (pointing to CHREMES’S house), if it suits you in any way.
(Moves toward the house.)
DEMIPHO:
(to CHREMES.)
Follow him, and hold him back, till I call out the servants.
CHREMES:
(trying to seize PHORMIO.)
But I can’t by myself; run and help me.
PHORMIO:
(to DEMIPHO, who seizes hold of him.)

Not for you, indeed; but there’s need for her to know it. At Lemnos —
CHREMES:
(starting.)
Ha! what are you doing?
DEMIPHO:
(to PHORMIO.)
Won’t you hold your tongue?
PHORMIO:
(to NAUSISTRATA.)
Unknown to you—
CHREMES:
Ah me!
PHORMIO:
He married another—
NAUSISTRATA:
My dear sir, may the Gods forbid it!

I’ faith, it is as you deserve.
PHORMIO:
First, then, will you do this, Nausistrata, at once, to please me, and to make your husband’s eyes ache with vexation?
NAUSISTRATA:
With all my heart.
PHORMIO:
Invite me to dinner.
NAUSISTRATA:
Assuredly indeed, I do invite you.
DEMIPHO:
Let us now away in-doors.
CHREMES:
By all means; but where is Phaedria, our arbitrator?
PHORMIO:
I’ll have him here just now.

> On the beautiful peak of Mount Kailāśa, Maheśvara was seated,
> and to Vṛhaspati he spoke of the unsurpassed truth of Śiva. || 1
> O venerable one, O God of gods, O beginningless supreme Lord,
> explain fully the whole *tattva* (reality) that delights all things moving and unmoving. || 2
> Well said, well said, O great being! The truth of the fruit of karma
> is indeed endowed with existence, both here and in the hereafter. || 3
> Blind men, accompanied by other blind men, in order to grasp the body of an elephant,
> not having perceived its true form with their eyes, are led into delusion by one another. || 4
> O venerable one, knower of all *tattva*, O beginningless supreme Lord,
> from you I wish to hear this, O venerable one, the entirety of *tattva*. || 5
> The supreme *tattva* is twofold: *cetana* and *acetana*.

> It pervades all *tattvas*, is subtle, and must be discerned with effort. || 6
> Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, imperishable,
> subtle, all-pervading, eternal, steadfast, immutable, sovereign. || 7
> Immeasurable due to infinity, indescribable due to being without attributes.
> Incomparable due to being without likeness, imperishable due to being stainless. || 8
> Subtle due to being imperceptible, and all-pervading due to being omnipresent.
> By its eternal nature it is void, and due to its immobility it is steadfast. || 9
> Immutable due to its completeness, and likewise of a tranquil nature.
> This is called *Śivatattva*, all-pervading and established everywhere. || 10
> Active, Śiva is the sun, the *tattva* of consciousness is Sadāśiva.
> He has a seat, has qualities, is pervasive, and is described as formless. || 11

> He is a creator, not an instrument; He is devoted to bestowing grace.
> He is ever-illuminating, all-knowing, all-doing, the omnipresent Lord. || 12
> For the shelterless, He is a brother; He is considered mother and father.
> He is the liberator from all sorrows, in every single birth. || 13
> This world is woven as warp and woof by Śiva, the supreme ruler.
> *Ūta* means pervaded, and *prota* is like jewels on a string. || 14
> *Sattva* is light and illuminating, *rajas* is established as restless,
> and *tamas* is heavy and obscuring; this is the mark of the mind-stuff. || 15
> *Mokṣa*, heaven, and hell, the state of animals and of humans,
> are born from the defilements of the mind-stuff, from the power of the mind-stuff. || 16
> Uprightness, non-attachment, gentleness, generosity,

> lordliness, skillfulness, sweetness, and a beautiful appearance. || 17
> Cruelty, arrogance, recklessness, ferocity,
> greed, fickleness, mercilessness, and heedlessness. || 18
> Laziness, fearfulness, lethargy, sleep, violence, heedlessness,
> sorrow, gluttony, gloominess, and constant bondage. || 19
> The extremely *sāttvika citta*, stainless and internally supreme,
> made of the nature of space, is pledged to all *mokṣa*. || 20
> The equilibrium of *rajas* is said to be for *dharma*, through which it desires good.
> Why is it conjoined with *sattva*? That indeed is the path to heaven. || 21
> The mind-stuff deluded by the *triguṇa*, from the beginning a blinding agent,
> its nature being why it is impure, its desired fruit is the human state. || 22
> The extremely *rājasa citta* is attached only to wrath and the like.

> It is born from fire; who indeed is the sevenfold one made of fire? || 23
> The extremely *tāmasa citta*, given to sleep, utterly deluded,
> swiftly enters the immobile state; this is certainly the work of the *citta*. || 24
> Good conduct, sacrifice, austerity, charity, renunciation, and the life of a mendicant.
> And yoga, in brief, is the one determination of *dharma*. || 25
> *Pratyakṣa*, *anumāna*, and the word of scripture from the final authority,
> are declared the threefold *pramāṇa*; that is the supreme, correct knowledge. || 26
> Towards pleasures seen and heard, towards the joys of the body, there is dispassion.
> That is known as *vairāgya*; the yogī is without desire for enjoyment. || 27
> In enjoyments, secondary enjoyments, and tertiary enjoyments as well,

> a commonality in all three is to be known by the wise as *aiśvarya*. || 28
> Through *dharma*, one goes to heaven; one is born into the womb of a god.
> Endowed with the powers of Aṇimā and the rest, one is satisfied in all enjoyments. || 29
> From correct knowledge, indeed, at will, the wise one has the four powers.
> Having attained the state of *mokṣa*, he does not enter existence again. || 30
> Through *vairāgya*, one is absorbed in *prakṛti*; one obtains happiness as if asleep.
> And after a long time, one is born into the womb of a god. || 31
> Through *aiśvarya*, one is unobstructed and satisfied by every enjoyment.
> Endowed with the powers of Aṇimā and the rest, one is born into the womb of a god. || 32
> Charity, study, the word, reasoning, and friendship,
> and the three destructions of suffering, are declared the eight perfections. || 33

> The body is like a cart, the soul is like an ox.
> Joined with Īśa as the charioteer, the world revolves like a wheel. || 34
> The body is called a palace, the three inner faculties are declared the ministers.
> The senses are called the servants, and the sense objects are like the pleasure of enjoyment. || 35
> Now I shall declare the *nāḍīs*; listen, they are three more than ten.
> In the navel, below the navel, in a bulb, they emerge, named from *ahaṅkāra*. || 36
> Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and then Suṣumnā there shall be.
> Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā and also Yaśā. || 37
> Alambuṣā and Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
> I shall now declare, O hero, the scriptural traditions of the *nāḍīs*. || 38
> These ten principal *nāḍīs* are remembered as the carriers of the vital airs.

> Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, and Udāna and Vyāna as well, || 39
> Nāga, Kūrma, and then Kṛkara, Devadatta, Dhanañjaya.
> These ten vital airs are thus declared and defined by Śiva. || 40
> Prāṇa is in the mouth, Apāna is below, Samāna is established in the heart.
> Udāna is known to be in the head, and Vyāna is in all the joints of the body. || 41
> The downward-moving air, Apāna, is established by which in the semen and urine. || 42
> It makes the eaten and drunk into bile, blood, and also phlegm.
> The movement in the limbs is equal; it is the air named Samāna. || 43
> It agitates the vital spots; it is the air named Udāna. || 44
> Vyāna is declared to be distinct; Vyāna is the agitator of disease.
> It is the agent of activity and agitation; old age comes from this air. || 45

> Nāga is said to be in belching, Kūrma is established in blinking.
> Kṛkara is in sneezing, and Devadatta is in yawning. || 46
> The gross waking state is variously composed and seen by direct perception.
> The dream state is like foam, waves, and bubbles, like an illusion, and fickle.
> The deep sleep state is a thicket of gloom and darkness, unmanifest and absolute.
> The fourth state is subtle, unthinkable, immutable; this the wise call *nirvāṇa*. || 47
> Freed from the state of being, and devoid of the state of non-being,
> beyond both being and non-being, formless, endless, and without characteristics. || 48
> As ghee is in milk, and Hari is in wood, water is in the sky, and the all-pervading wind,
> as *rajas* and *tamas* are unseen in the mind of a man, so He is neither being nor non-being; in the external world, He is not found. || 49

> This son is greatly skilled, and also a knower of the science of *tattva*.
> Vṛhaspati is spoken of here, the wise mendicant of heaven. || 50
> What is the path, the means, the knowledge? What is the supreme austerity and vow?
> O Śiva, having revered the supreme, you must explain this to me in truth. || 51
> From the pre-eminence of knowledge, *mokṣa* is attained; from the path of non-contact with the senses,
> and from the destruction of the fault of craving—it is obtained from these three causes. || 52
> *Pratyāhāra* and also *dhyāna*, *prāṇāyāma* and *dhāraṇa*,
> and *tarka* as well as *samādhi*—this is called the six-limbed yoga. || 53
> Withdrawing the senses from their objects, from the objects of the senses, with effort,
> by means of a tranquil mind, is called *pratyāhāra*. || 54

> Without duality, without modification, tranquil, and also unmoving,
> that form which one meditates on constantly, that is said to be *dhyāna*. || 55
> Having closed all the gates, the vital air is restrained within.
> Piercing the crown of the head with the vital air, it is called *prāṇāyāma*. || 56
> Placing the OṀ in the heart, absorbed in the *tattva*, of the nature of Śiva,
> because the OṀ is held, it is indeed called *dhāraṇa*. || 57
> Like space is that form, space is continuous and steadfast.
> One should constantly investigate that which is soundless; that is said to be *tarka*. || 58
> Without expectation, without conception, without craving, tranquil, immutable,
> one should constantly contemplate the uncharacterizable; by that it is called *samādhi*. || 59

> *Ahiṃsā*, *brahmacarya*, and *satya*, non-worldliness,
> and non-stealing—these five are the restraints (*yama*) spoken by Rudra. || 60
> Non-anger, service to the guru, purity, lightness of food,
> and non-heedlessness—these five are declared the observances (*niyama*). || 61
> Earth, and then water, fire and also air,
> space, intellect, and mind—listen, this is called the seven limbs. || 62
> The smeller, the taster, the seer, the feeler, and the hearer,
> the conceiver and the knower as well, listen—this is called the seven fires. || 63
> Sound, touch, and form, and taste and smell are said to be,
> conception and what is to be known as well—this is called the seven nectars. || 64
> This god, this fire, burns the heap of sins well-accumulated.
> He then fulfills all wishes, for Śiva is like a wish-fulfilling gem. || 65

> *Aṇimā* and *laghimā* as well, *mahimā* and *prāpti* also,
> and *prākāmya* and *īśitva*, *vaśitva* and *yatrakāmatva*. || 66
> As the body becomes extremely subtle, having abandoned the gross at will,
> he of three bodies, *aṇimā*, goes forth; by this he is called ‘aṇimā’. || 67
> What was formerly heavy, having abandoned that in an instant,
> the body becomes light as cotton at will; thus this is *laghimā*. || 68
> Wherever he goes at will, there he is honored according to his will.
> Because he is worshipped everywhere, by that it is called *mahimā*. || 69
> As if from a treasury, he obtains the object he has gone to.
> For the attainment of all things, the name here is *prāpti* everywhere. || 70
> The form made by the self is obtained by the self.
> Whatever form is made at will, that is declared *prākāmya*. || 71

> If he always goes to the realms of Brahma, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Sūrya,
> for the sake of devotion favorable to the gods, the name *īśitva* is spoken. || 72
> Wherever there is control, from control comes the ability to go where one wills. || 73
> The will to go with the body is *yatrakāmāvasāyitva*. || 74b

"The gods' renowned gifts are not to be cast away,
all that they themselves bestow — though no man would take them of his own will,"
Calpurnianus, greetings in these hurried lines.
I have sent you, as you asked, a thing to make your teeth shine clean,
a polish for the mouth, from the fruits of Arabia,
a fine, white, noble little powder,
a smoother of the swollen little gum,
a sweeper-away of yesterday's leavings,
that no foul stain of grime may show
if perchance, with parted lips, you should smile.
And Critias is my delight, and you, Charinus, my well-being,
a part in my love remains for you, my life;
fear nothing; for though fire and fire scorch me as it will,
these two flames, so I may possess them, I will endure.
On this condition may I be to you what each is to himself:

this you shall be to me, what the two eyes are.
Garlands of flowers, my honey, and these songs I give you.
Songs I give to you, garlands to your guardian spirit,
songs, that this longed-for day, Critias, may be sung,
the day that returns to you each fourteenth spring;
and the garlands, that your temples may bloom in this glad season,
that you may adorn the flower of your youth with flowers.
You in return give me your springtime for my springtime flower,
that you may outdo my gifts with gifts of your own;
for the woven garlands you shall give an embrace of your body,
and for the roses, the kisses of your crimson lips.
But should you breathe your soul into the reed-pipe, then my songs
shall yield, conquered by your sweet-voiced reed.
Aster, once you shone among the living as the Morning Star;

now, dead, you shine as the Evening Star among the departed.
Now, when Alexis is no more than this — that one said only he was fair —
he is gazed at, and on every side by all is admired.
My heart,
why point out the bone to the dogs? You will suffer for it
afterward. Was it not thus we lost Phaedrus?
For it is fitting that the dutiful poet himself be chaste,
but for his little verses there is no such need.
"There is a city in the midst of the wine-dark mist..."
Plants of ripening growth, with the milk of black poison,
are sought, reaped by moonlight with bronze sickles;
sought too is the love-charm torn from the forehead of a new-born foal,
snatched away before its mother could seize it.
31. all manner of love-charms they dig up from everywhere:
the famous "antipathes" is sought,

little wheels, nail-parings, fillets,
little roots, herbs, twigs,
two-tailed lizards as decoys,
the lure of whinnying mares.
As the sea-weasel of Clupea surpasses all,
so the mussels of Aenus, and the rough oysters most plentiful at Abydus.
At Mytilene is the scallop, and near Ambracia the boar-fish of Charadrus.
At Brundisium the bream is good; if it be large, take it.
Know that the boar-fish is best at Tarentum;
at Surrentum see you buy the sturgeon, and the glaucus at Cumae.
And why have I passed over the parrot-wrasse, the very brain, almost, of supreme Jove —
(this is caught, big and good, near the homeland of Nestor) —
the black-tail, the thrush-wrasse, the merle-wrasse, and the sea-shade.
At Corcyra the polyp, and the fat skulls of the maigre,
the purple-fish, the little murex, the mussels, and the sweet sea-urchins too.
